subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4! In this unit you will explore the world of three-dimensional shapes – the solid shapes we call 3D shapes for short. Look around you right now. The box that holds Amina's dates, the ball Yusuf kicks in the football match, the tin of tomatoes on the shelf at the Hargeisa market, the cone of an ice-cream at a family celebration – every one of them is a 3D shape. Unlike flat shapes drawn on paper, 3D shapes take up real space in the world. You can pick them up, turn them around, and hold them in your hands.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

outcomes: Identify and name common 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone, prism and pyramid.
Describe a 3D shape by its faces, edges and vertices.
Explain the difference between a prism and a pyramid.
Recognise 3D shapes in everyday objects around you.
Sort and classify 3D shapes by their properties.
Understand and use nets – the flat patterns that fold into solid shapes.
Sketch simple 3D shapes and label their features.

Name and classify 2D shapes, including regular and irregular polygons such as pentagons, hexagons and octagons, by their sides, vertices and right angles, and relate them to the flat faces you see in drawings of 3D shapes.

concepts.title: What Makes a Shape 3D?
concepts.explanation: A flat shape, like a square or a circle drawn on paper, has only two measurements: how long it is and how wide it is. We call these 2D shapes, which is short for two-dimensional. You can draw them but you cannot pick them up off the page. A 3D shape is different. It has three measurements: length, width and height. Because it has height as well, it stands up off the page and takes up space in the world. The word for the space a solid shape takes up is volume. A drawing of a box on paper is 2D, but the real box… Flat shapes have their own names and families too, and it helps to know them well before you study solids. A shape is called regular when all of its sides are the same length and all of its angles are the same size — like a square, where every side is equal and every corner is a right angle. A shape is irregular when its sides and angles are not all equal, even though it may have the same number of sides — for example, a triangle with three different side lengths, or a hexagon whose sides are not all the same. You can sort any flat shape by counting its sides and its vertices (corners): a triangle has 3 sides and 3 vertices, a quadrilateral such as a square, rectangle or parallelogram has 4 of each, a pentagon has 5, a hexagon has 6, and an octagon has 8. A semicircle is made by cutting a circle exactly in half along one straight line, so it has one straight side and one curved side. You can also sort flat shapes by counting their right angles: a square and a rectangle each have 4 right angles, a right-angled triangle has exactly 1, and a circle or a semicircle has none, because neither one has a straight corner. Whenever you draw a 3D shape like a cube or a cuboid on paper, you are really drawing several 2D shapes joined together — a drawing of a cube is really six squares arranged to look solid, and a drawing of a triangular prism shows triangles and rectangles side by side, which is exactly why the flat faces of every 3D shape are always 2D shapes.
concepts.example: Every solid 3D shape can be described using three special features. Learn these three words well, because you will use them in every single lesson of this unit:

concepts.title: The Common 3D Shapes
concepts.explanation:
Now let us meet the family of common 3D shapes one by one. As you read about each, try to picture a real object from your home or the market that has that shape. Holding the real thing while you read makes the shape stick in your memory.

A cube has 6 faces, and every single face is a square of exactly the same size. It has 12 edges, and all twelve are the same length. It has 8 vertices. A die is a perfect cube, and so is a sugar cube or a child's building block. Because all its faces are equal squares, a cube looks the same whichever way you turn it.

A cuboid also has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, just like a cube. But on a cuboid the faces are rectangles, and they are not all the same size. A cereal box, a book, a brick, and the box that Hassan's new shoes came in are all cuboids. A cube is really a special cuboid where every face happens to be a square – so every cube is a cuboid, but not every cuboid is a cube.

A sphere is a perfectly round ball. It has just one curved surface, and it has no edges and no vertices at all. A football, an orange, and a globe of the world are all spheres. Because it is round all over, a sphere will roll in any direction.

A cylinder has two flat circular faces – one at the top and one at the bottom – joined by one curved surface around the side. It has 2 edges (the circles at the top and bottom) and no vertices. A tin of tomatoes, a drinking cup, and a candle are all cylinders. A cylinder can roll on its side but stands firm on its flat ends.

A cone has one flat circular face at the bottom and one curved surface that rises to a single point at the top. That point is called the apex, and it is the shape's one vertex. A cone has 1 edge, where the curved surface meets the circle. An ice-cream cone and a party hat are cones. So is a traditional funnel used to pour cooking oil.

A triangular prism has 5 faces: 2 triangular faces at the ends and 3 rectangular faces joining them. It has 9 edges and 6 vertices. A Toblerone chocolate box is a triangular prism, and so is a camping tent standing on the ground with its triangular ends open.

A square-based pyramid has 5 faces: 1 square face at the bottom (the base) and 4 triangular faces that lean in and meet at a single point at the top. It has 8 edges and 5 vertices. The great pyramids of Egypt are the most famous example in the world.

concepts.title: Counting Faces, Edges and Vertices Carefully
concepts.explanation:
Counting the faces, edges and vertices of a shape sounds easy, but it is very simple to lose your place and count the same edge twice, or miss a hidden one at the back. Good mathematicians count in an organised way so nothing is missed and nothing is counted twice. Let us learn a careful method using a cube.

To count the faces of a cube, imagine the cube as a box. Count the top and the bottom – that is 2. Count the front and the back – that is 2 more, making 4. Count the left and the right – that is the last 2, making 6 faces in all. Working around the shape in pairs like this stops you from forgetting the face you cannot see at the back.

To count the edges, count the 4 edges around the top square, then the 4 edges around the bottom square – that is 8 so far. Then count the 4 upright edges that join the top to the bottom. That gives 8 + 4 = 12 edges. To count the vertices, count the 4 corners of the top square and the 4 corners of the bottom square: 4 + 4 = 8 vertices.
concepts.example: The same careful habit works for any shape. For a square-based pyramid, count the 4 corners of the square base, then add the single apex at the top: 4 + 1 = 5 vertices. For the edges, count the 4 edges around the square base, then the 4 slanting edges climbing to the apex: 4 + 4 = 8 edges. When Khadija counts slowly and in order like this, she gets the right answer every time.

concepts.title: Understanding Prisms
concepts.explanation:
A prism is a very special kind of 3D shape. A prism has:

Two identical ends that are exactly the same shape and the same size. These ends are called the bases.

Flat faces all around – a prism has no curved surfaces.

The same cross-section all the way through. This means if you slice the prism anywhere between its two ends, the slice is always the same shape.

Think of a loaf of bread that is the same shape from one end to the other. Every slice you cut is the same rectangle. That is what makes it a prism. A tent whose two triangular ends match exactly, with straight sides joining them, is a triangular prism – every slice from front to back is the same triangle.
concepts.example: Prisms are named after the shape of their bases. This is a very useful rule, because once you can name the base you can name the whole prism. For example, a triangular prism has triangular bases; a rectangular prism (a cuboid) has rectangular bases; a hexagonal prism has six-sided bases. Even a cube is a prism – its bases are squares, so it is really a special square prism. When Ibrahim looks at a new prism, the first thing he does is look at the two matching ends and ask, ‘What shape are they?’ That answer names the shape.

concepts.title: Understanding Pyramids
concepts.explanation:
A pyramid is another special 3D shape, but it is built in a very different way from a prism. A pyramid has:

One base, which can be any flat polygon – a triangle, a square, a pentagon and so on.

Triangular faces that rise up from the edges of the base and all meet at a single point.

That meeting point at the top is called the apex.

Picture the great pyramids near Cairo. They sit on a square base, and four triangular walls climb up and meet at a point high in the sky. That is a square-based pyramid. Like prisms, pyramids are named after the shape of their base. A triangular pyramid has a triangular base; a square-based pyramid has a square base; a pentagonal pyramid has a five-sided base.
concepts.example: Here is the big difference to hold in your mind. A prism has two identical ends and looks the same all the way through. A pyramid has only one base and rises to a single point, so it gets narrower as it goes up. If Zahra builds a shape that comes to a sharp point at the top, it is a pyramid. If she builds a shape with two matching ends and straight sides, it is a prism.

concepts.title: Sorting and Classifying 3D Shapes
concepts.explanation:
Because there are so many 3D shapes, mathematicians like to sort them into groups. Sorting means putting shapes together that share a property. There is no single right way to sort – it depends on which property you choose. Here are some useful ways to sort the shapes you have met:

Shapes with only flat faces (cube, cuboid, prisms, pyramids) versus shapes with at least one curved surface (sphere, cylinder, cone).

Shapes with at least one triangular face (triangular prism, pyramids) versus shapes with no triangular faces (cube, cuboid, cylinder).

Prisms (two matching ends) versus pyramids (one base and an apex).

Shapes that can roll (sphere, cylinder, cone) versus shapes that cannot roll (cube, cuboid).

A clever tool for sorting is a Venn diagram – two overlapping circles. You choose a property for each circle. For example, one circle could be curved surface and the other could be has a vertex. A cone has both a curved surface and a vertex, so it belongs in the overlap where the circles cross. A sphere has a curved surface but no vertex, so it goes in the curved circle only. A cube has neither, so it stays outside both circles. Sorting like this helps you see clearly how shapes are alike and how they differ.
concepts.example: Sorting is not just a classroom game. When Omar stacks goods in his shop, he keeps the cuboids together because they pile up neatly, and he keeps the round tins and cans in a row where they will not roll away. He is sorting 3D shapes by their properties every single day without even thinking of it as maths.

methods.title: Look at the faces: are they flat, curved, or both?
methods.example: A shape has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, and all its faces are squares. What is it?
steps: Count the faces in an organised order (top, bottom, sides).
Count the edges where faces meet.
Count the vertices (corners).
Decide: is it a prism, a pyramid, or neither? Then name it.

methods.title: How to tell a prism from a pyramid
methods.example: How many faces, edges and vertices does a triangular prism have?
steps: Look for two identical ends. If they are there, it is a prism.
Look for a single point at the top (an apex). If it is there, it is a pyramid.
Name the shape after its base: triangular, square, hexagonal, and so on.

methods.title: How to use a net
methods.example: How many faces, edges and vertices does a triangular prism have?
steps: Imagine unfolding the shape until it lies flat.
Count the flat faces you can see in the net.
Fold it back in your mind to check it makes the solid shape.

methods.title: Identify from a real object
methods.example: What 3D shape is a tin of tomatoes at the market?
steps: A tin has a flat circle at the top, a flat circle at the bottom, and a curved surface around the side.
A shape with two circular faces and one curved surface is a cylinder.
Check by looking for the same shape features (two circular faces, one curved side) in another real object, like a drum.

methods.title: Use the base to name a prism
methods.example: A prism has two identical hexagonal (six-sided) ends. What is its name?
steps: Prisms are named after the shape of their base.
The base is a hexagon, so the shape is a hexagonal prism.

workedExamples.title: Name the shape from its features
workedExamples.prompt: A shape has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, and all its faces are squares. What is it?
workedExamples.solution: Six faces, twelve edges and eight vertices could be a cube or a cuboid — those numbers are the same for both. The extra clue is that all the faces are squares. Only a cube has all-square faces, so the shape is a cube.

workedExamples.title: Count the parts of a triangular prism
workedExamples.prompt: How many faces, edges and vertices does a triangular prism have?
workedExamples.solution: Count in an organised way. Faces: 2 triangular ends + 3 rectangles joining them = 5 faces. Vertices: 3 corners on the front triangle + 3 corners on the back triangle = 6 vertices. Edges: 3 around the front triangle + 3 around the back triangle + 3 joining them = 9 edges. A triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

workedExamples.title: Prism or pyramid?
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan has a shape with a square base and four triangular faces meeting at a point. Is it a prism or a pyramid, and what is its name?
workedExamples.solution: It has one base and comes to a single point (apex), so it is a pyramid. Since its base is a square, it is called a square-based pyramid (or square pyramid).

workedExamples.title: Identify from a real object
workedExamples.prompt: What 3D shape is a tin of tomatoes at the market?
workedExamples.solution: A tin has a flat circle at the top, a flat circle at the bottom, and a curved surface around the side. A shape with two circular faces and one curved surface is a cylinder.

workedExamples.title: Use the base to name a prism
workedExamples.prompt: A prism has two identical hexagonal (six-sided) ends. What is its name?
workedExamples.solution: Prisms are named after the shape of their base. The base is a hexagon, so the shape is a hexagonal prism.

workedExamples.title: Curved or flat?
workedExamples.prompt: Sort these into curved-surface shapes and flat-face-only shapes: cube, sphere, cone, cuboid, cylinder.
workedExamples.solution: A cube and a cuboid have only flat faces. A sphere, cone and cylinder each have at least one curved surface. So: flat only = cube, cuboid; curved = sphere, cone, cylinder.

workedExamples.title: Count the net
workedExamples.prompt: Yusuf unfolds a shape and sees 1 square and 4 triangles lying flat. Which shape did it come from?
workedExamples.solution: One square base and four triangular faces fold up to a single point. That is a square-based pyramid.

workedExamples.title: Compare two shapes
workedExamples.prompt: Write one thing that is the same and one thing that is different about a cube and a square-based pyramid.
workedExamples.solution: Same: both have flat faces and both have a square somewhere (the cube has square faces; the pyramid has a square base). Different: a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, while a square-based pyramid has only 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices — and the pyramid rises to a point while the cube does not.

workedExamples.title: True or False
workedExamples.prompt: True or False: a) a sphere has one curved surface b) a cone has two vertices c) a cube is a special cuboid.
workedExamples.solution: a) True, b) False (a cone has 1 vertex, the apex), c) True.

workedExamples.title: A prism has two identical ends shaped like pentagons…
workedExamples.prompt: A prism has two identical ends shaped like pentagons. What is its name and how many rectangular side faces does it have?
workedExamples.solution: A pentagonal prism; it has 5 rectangular side faces.

workedExamples.title: Which shapes have at least one triangular face: cube…
workedExamples.prompt: Which shapes have at least one triangular face: cube, triangular prism, square-based pyramid, cylinder?
workedExamples.solution: Triangular prism and square-based pyramid have triangular faces.

workedExamples.title: A shape has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices. One face…
workedExamples.prompt: A shape has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices. One face is a square and the rest are triangles. Name it and describe it.
workedExamples.solution: A square-based pyramid: it has 1 square base and 4 triangular faces meeting at an apex, with 8 edges and 5 vertices.

activities.title: Shape Detectives
steps: Walk around your home and the courtyard looking for 3D shapes.
For each shape you find, write down the name of the shape, the object it is part of, and how many faces, edges and vertices it has.
Try to find at least ten different 3D shapes.
Challenge: Sort your shapes into groups. How many different ways can you group them – by flat or curved, by can roll or cannot roll, by prism or pyramid?
This activity trains your eyes to see the mathematics hidden in everyday objects.

activities.title: Build-a-Shape with Straws and Clay
activities.materials: straws or thin sticks for the edges, and small balls of clay, dough or dates for the vertices.
steps: Use straws as edges and clay balls as vertices.
Build a cube, then a triangular prism, then a square-based pyramid.
For each shape, count how many straws (edges) and how many clay balls (vertices) you used, and write them down.
Challenge: Can you build a shape with exactly 9 edges? What about exactly 6 vertices? (Hint: think about the triangular prism.)

activities.title: The Shape Feely Bag
activities.materials: a cloth bag or pillowcase, and several small 3D objects (a die, a tin, a ball, a small box, a party hat).
steps: Put the objects into the bag without letting your partner see.
Your partner reaches in, feels one object, and describes its faces, edges and vertices out loud – without looking.
From the description, they must name the shape before pulling it out to check.
Swap over and take turns. Who can name the most shapes just by touch?
Feeling shapes with your hands helps you truly understand faces, edges and vertices.

activities.title: Make a Net (Investigation)
activities.materials: an empty cardboard box (a small cereal or tea box), scissors, and a pencil.
steps: Carefully open the box along its glued edges until it lies completely flat. Ask an adult to help with the cutting.
Look at the flat shape – this is the net of the box. Count how many rectangles you can see.
Draw around your flattened box on paper to record its net, then fold it back up into the cuboid.
Challenge: Can you draw a net for a cube using 6 squares? Cut it out and fold it to test whether it works.

activities.title: Prism to Pyramid (Family Task)
activities.materials: straws and clay, and a family member to work with.
steps: Together, build a triangular prism. Count the straws and clay balls you used (you should need 9 straws and 6 clay balls).
Now change it into a triangular pyramid by removing straws and clay. Count what you use now (6 straws and 4 clay balls).
Talk about how the two shapes are the same and how they are different.
Challenge: Try the same with a square base. Build a shape with a square base as a prism, then rebuild it as a square-based pyramid, and compare.

activities.title: 3D Shape Property Game
activities.materials: a die, some paper shape cards you draw yourself, and counters (stones or bottle caps).
steps: Write six properties on a paper key, numbered 1 to 6 to match the die: all faces flat, has a curved surface, has a triangular face, has a square face, has no vertices, has an apex.
Roll the die and read the matching property from your key.
Place a counter on one shape card that has that property. Each card can hold only one counter.
Keep playing until all the cards are covered. The winner is the player with the most counters.

rules.title: Prism Naming Rule
rules.text: Prisms are named after the shape of their bases. This is a very useful rule, because once you can name the base you can name the whole prism. For example, a triangular prism has triangular bases; a rectangular prism (a cuboid) has rectangular bases; a hexagonal prism has six-sided bases. Even a cube is a prism – its bases are squares, so it is really a special square prism. When Ibrahim looks at a new prism, the first thing he does is look at the two matching ends and ask, What shape are they? That answer names the shape.

Count in order; include what you cannot see
Curved surface is not a face
Faces depend on the base shape

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Understanding Pyramids.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A pyramid is another special 3D shape, but it is built in a very different way from a prism. A pyramid has: One base, which can be any flat polygon – a triangle, a square, a pentagon and so on.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Sorting and Classifying 3D Shapes.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because there are so many 3D shapes, mathematicians like to sort them into groups. Sorting means putting shapes together that share a property. There is no single right way to sort – it depends on which property you choose. Here are some useful ways to sort the shapes you have met: Shapes with only flat faces (cube, cuboid, prisms, pyramids) versus shapes with at least one curved surface (sphere, cylinder, cone).

I can recognise 3D shapes in everyday objects around me.
I can sort and classify 3D shapes by their properties.
I can understand and use nets – the flat patterns that fold into solid shapes.
I can sketch simple 3D shapes and label their features.
